column4: The section casts the moon as the sun's follower (source-section root ت ل و); `لا الشمس ينبغي لها أن تدرك القمر` sets their order by saying the sun does not overtake the moon.
The source-section noun/root `ناقة` identifies the same animal: Ṣāliḥ names her as God's sign, permits her to graze, and forbids harm, the boundary the later hamstringing crosses.
This repeats the she-camel as God's sign and the command to let her graze untouched; its ban makes the offense in 11:65 legible.
`ثمود الناقة مبصرة` presents the she-camel as a visible sign and says Thamud wronged it; this joins the body's injury to the sign's rejection.
`هذه ناقة لها شرب ولكم شرب يوم معلوم` gives the camel and people separate allotted drinking turns, matching the source-section's `س ق ي` / watering detail.
The warning `ولا تمسوها بسوء` draws a boundary around the camel before 26:157 recounts the hamstringing; this ayah contributes the explicit prohibition and threatened consequence.
`إنا مرسلو الناقة فتنة لهم` sends the she-camel as a test; the source-section root `ر س ل` links the messenger's name with the camel's easy movement, while this verse makes sending her the trial.
The water is divided between them and each drinking turn is attended; this is the same camel-water arrangement named by `وسقياها` in the source section.
`فعقروا الناقة` is the same assault; the source-section root `ع ق ر` is glossed there as cutting the camel's hock tendon.
`فعقروها` names the camel's hamstringing, matching the source-section's specific bodily gloss of root `ع ق ر`.
`فعقروها` repeats the hamstringing and adds that they became remorseful; the root `ع ق ر` keeps the act located in the camel's body.
After they call their companion, `فتعاطى فعقر` singles out the agent who takes up the act; it matches the source-section's lone wretched man and root `ع ق ر`.
The quake seizes the people immediately after 7:77's hamstringing; this supplies the consequence that the source section says follows the camel's injury.
The cry seizes the wrongdoers after 11:65's injury; the verse gives the collective aftermath of the bodily act.
`فأخذهم العذاب` follows the camel's killing in 26:157, supplying the punishment after the offense that the source section's sequence anticipates.
The single cry comes after the companion hamstrings the camel in 54:29; it completes this retelling's consequence.
This asks how severe God's punishment and warning were, directly interpreting the camel episode and the cry that follows it in 54:31.
The closing words call the episode a sign; its own contribution is to frame the camel's fate and punishment as a warning, with 26:155–158 giving the specific events.

The source-section distinguishes cutting the sign-camel's hock from the later lexical use of `ع ق ر` for slaughter at the throat; 22:36 describes sacrificial camels whose fallen sides become food to share, a distinct camel's bodily fate.

The source-section's root `ب ع ث` describes both a driver raising a camel and its own rising; here `ثم بعثه` describes the man restored to life by God, and the ayah then directs him to look at his donkey and at bones being reassembled and clothed in flesh, contrasting an externally caused raising with 91:12's camel rising without a raiser.
`من بعثنا من مرقدنا` uses the source-section root `ب ع ث` for people awakened at resurrection; it contrasts the camel's ordinary arising in 91:12 with a raising that requires an agent.
The source-section's root `ل ه م` has a secondary dictionary gloss for a young animal taking milk at its mother's teat; `أرضعيه` gives a human mother nursing Moses, a specific nursing parallel.

The source-section's root `ل ه م` has a secondary dictionary gloss for a young animal nursing at its mother; this ayah directly describes mothers nursing their children and so supplies the human counterpart.
The source-section's root `ل ه م` has a secondary dictionary gloss for a young animal at its mother's teat; this ayah describes mothers nursing children and the care owed for that act.

The section's moon-after-sun sequence belongs to a larger ordered cycle; `يكور الليل على النهار` and the sun and moon running to appointed terms show the paired bodies and day-night succession around it.
The moon follows the sun in the section's ordered sky, while `وجمع الشمس والقمر` brings the same pair together at the Last Hour, a specific reversal of their ordinary relation.
The section calls the camel's attacker `أشقاها`; here `ويتجنبها الأشقى` applies “most wretched” to the one who avoids the reminder, tying that label to rejection of warning.
`الأشقى` again names the one who reaches the great Fire, extending the source section's label for the camel's attacker toward an outcome; 92:16 specifies his denial and turning away.

This identifies the wretched one as `الذي كذب وتولى`, a denial-and-turning-away pattern that clarifies the source section's statement that Thamud rejected Ṣāliḥ before attacking the sign; 92:15 gives the stated Fire outcome.
`كذبت ثمود بالنذر` states the community's rejection of warnings, the stance that leads into Ṣāliḥ's camel warning and their denial of him in the source section.
The people object to following one mortal from among them; this gives their resistance to Ṣāliḥ's warning, while 54:27 identifies the camel test at issue.
Their question about the reminder and accusation that he is a liar anticipates 91:14's denial of the messenger; 54:27 then makes the warning concrete through the camel.
The promised exposure of the liar and insolent anticipates the consequence after the camel test in 54:27–31; this ayah contributes the forecast before that sequence.
After the camel's injury and punishment, Ṣāliḥ says he delivered his Lord's message and advised them; this clarifies the messenger's warning role in 91:13.
After the camel's violation, God saves Ṣāliḥ and the believers; this supplies the other side of the outcome, distinct from the wrongdoers' fate in 11:67.
The next verse says it was as though Thamud had never lived there; it gives the scale of the aftermath after the camel's injury and the cry in 11:67.
`كذبت ثمود المرسلين` opens another account of the same community rejecting its messengers, matching the rejection of the messenger who names the camel in 91:13–14.
Ṣāliḥ asks whether they will fear God; this introduces the warning stance before 26:143 names him as messenger and 26:155–156 give the camel command.
Ṣāliḥ calls himself a trustworthy `رسول`; the source-section root `ر س ل` also describes an easy-moving camel, and 26:155–156 give this messenger's specific camel and water warning.
Ṣāliḥ commands them to fear God and obey him; 26:155–156 specify the camel-care command that the community violates.
Ṣāliḥ repeats “fear God and obey me” just before describing the camel; this frames the camel's protection as part of the command they reject.
He forbids obedience to the extravagant, which sharpens the opposition between his camel warning and the transgressive act in 26:157; 26:155–156 state the warning itself.
Those he warns against are described as spreading corruption and not setting things right; their treatment of the protected camel in 26:155–157 makes that description concrete.
The people answer Ṣāliḥ's warning by calling him bewitched; this is their resistance before he presents the camel in 26:155.
They demand a sign from Ṣāliḥ, which the following 26:155 identifies as the camel; this ayah supplies the challenge to which the camel responds.
The section's calf follows its mother; `مرضعة عما أرضعت` depicts the opposite boundary, a nursing mother losing awareness of the child at the terrors of the Hour.

The section pairs the moon with the sun in a following relation; this ayah says both move in their own orbits, giving the same celestial pair's ordered motion while leaving the section's specific follower relation distinct.

The source-section links root `ع ق ب` from the camel's hock to what follows an act; here `عقبى الدار` names a good outcome granted for patience, a counter-outcome to Thamud's violation after Ṣāliḥ is told to be patient in 54:27.

The source-section identifies `ع ق ب` with the camel's hock and the back of the foot; `على أعقابكم` uses heels for turning back if a messenger dies or is killed, making physical retreat resonate with the community's rejection of Ṣāliḥ's warning.

The source-section's root `ع ق ب` names the hock and heel; this ayah warns that following disbelievers can turn people `على أعقابكم`, a bodily image of retreat that reverses obedience to the messenger and his camel command.
The she-camel is a visible sign in 17:59; this account says Thamud preferred blindness over guidance and were struck for it, making their refusal of the sign a specific reversal of its visibility.

The camel in the source section rises without a handler, while this ayah says Thamud could not rise or defend themselves after punishment; 51:44 supplies the preceding disobedience and thunderbolt, and this verse contributes their helplessness.
